Perceiving Compliance in Virtual Reality: Effects of Interaction Direction and Sensory Discrepancy on Visuo-Haptic Weighting

Taehyeong Jung*, Jiwan Lee*, Junwoo Kim, Seungmoon Choi (* Equal contribution)

IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (IEEE TVCG), 2026 · Early Access · pp. 1–11

PaperCitation details

At a glance

When judging softness in VR, do people rely more on what they see or what they feel?

When a virtual object looks softer than it feels, the direction of the press can change which cue a person trusts. The effect depends on how far apart the visual and haptic cues are.

VRCompliance perceptionVisuo-haptic weighting

The approach

Participants judged the compliance of virtual objects while the displayed deformation and the force they felt implied different stiffnesses. The experiment compared two sizes of mismatch across three directions of interaction.

Key takeaways

  1. 01

    Vision carried more weight when pressing down

    With the larger mismatch, top-down judgments leaned more on the deformation people saw.

  2. 02

    Touch carried more weight front to back

    At that same mismatch, force feedback had more influence during front-back interaction. Side-to-side judgments drew more evenly on both cues.

  3. 03

    Smaller discrepancies reduced the directional effect

    Direction made little difference when the cues were closer together. The results suggest accounting for the direction of a press when deciding how to render a deformable object.
